entries.title: Bayeux Tapestry goes on display at sold-out London exhibit
entries.summary: The nearly 1,000 year-old, 70-meter-long tapestry is considered a symbol of UK-France friendship. More than 100,000 tickets have been sold.
entries.content:
September 10, 2026

The nearly 1,000 year-old, 70-meter-long tapestry is considered a symbol of UK-France friendship. More than 100,000 tickets have been sold.

The Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London opened Thursday to much fanfare, in what British newspaper the Times has dubbed "Tapestry-mania," with more than 100,000 tickets already sold.

The tapestry is on loan from France, and comes after years of diplomacy, with the move being seen as a symbol of close ties between Paris and London. It is thought to be the first time the tapestry has gone on display outside of France.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the tapestry's loan a "return," while King Charles III hailed the move as a "precious symbol of trust at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

The work is believed to have been made in England nearly 1,000 years ago before finding its way to Bayeux, now located in the French region of Normandy.

Two previous attempts to loan the Bayeux Tapestry to the UK were unsuccessful. Once was in 1953 for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and again in 1966 for the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings, which is depicted on the tapestry.

What is the Bayeux Tapestry?

The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millennium, and turned out to be the last one for a millennium

The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.

The Bayeux Tapestry will be on display at London's British Museum until next July.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy arrives in Canada seeking air support
entries.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the midst of a multi-nation tour to shore up his country's air defenses ahead of winter.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's Zelenskyy arrives in Canada seeking air support

September 10, 2026

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the midst of a multi-nation tour to shore up his country's air defenses ahead of winter.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary late on Wednesday for "important meetings ​and agreements" with Canadian officials, including Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Zelenskyy arrived on the heels on attending King Harald V's funeral in Norway, where his plane had been delayed by a drone incursion.

The Ukrainian leader is in the middle of a flurry of trips and meetings to shore up his country's defenses for the cold winter months. 

"The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter," Zelenskyy said in a social media post before leaving.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."

Carney's statement added Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."

Zelenskyy had also signaled a desire to meet with US President Donald Trump on the matter before the end of September.

Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Moscow has consistently increased attacks on fuel and heating infrastructure in Ukraine in the autumn and winter.

What is happening on the battlefield?

Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region overnight, as well as a seaport in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said. He added that other unnamed sited critical to Russia's war industry had also been hit.

Alexander Gusev, governor of Russia's Voronezh region, said that one woman in the town of Borisoglebsk had been killed by falling drone debris overnight and that at least 19 drones had been destroyed while flying over the region.

The Russian Defense Ministry said a total of 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ecuador: Ex-president Bucaram sentenced in corruption case
entries.summary: Abdala Bucaram, Ecuador's former president, was convicted for his role in the illegal sale of COVID-19 tests and medical supplies, receiving a prison sentence of over nine years.
entries.content:
Ecuador

Ecuador: Ex-president Bucaram sentenced in corruption case

September 10, 2026

Abdala Bucaram, Ecuador's former president, was convicted for his role in the illegal sale of COVID-19 tests and medical supplies, receiving a prison sentence of over nine years.

Abdala Bucaram, Ecuador's former president, was found guilty of corruption and sentenced on Wednesday to nine years and four months in prison for being "collaborators" in organized crime.

Bucaram's son, Jacob Bucaram, was also sentenced for the illegal sale of at least21,000 COVID-19 tests and other medical supplies during the pandemic in 2020. 

The trial, which lasted six years, continued following an appeal from the attorney general's office, after a judge dismissed the charges against Bucaram and his son in 2021.

What are the details of the case?

Bucaram heard the decision remotely from a guarded clinic in Guayaquil where he was receiving medical care.

At 74 years old, he may serve his ⁠sentence ​under house ​arrest due to ​his age, in ‌accordance with Ecuadorean law.

He was arrested in 2020 following a raid on his home in Guayaquil, and was put under house arrest as he could not initially be imprisoned due to health problems.

The former president has undergone surgery for heart issues and was admitted to intensive care.

Bucaram posted a message on X stating that he had requested to be discharged from the clinic "despite being at risk of sudden death."

"I will be able to defend myself, and the country will learn horrifying things about this process," he added.

According to the investigation,COVID-19 tests were illegally transferred to Bucaram's residence, which was guarded by Quito traffic agents.

According to the public prosecutor's office, the tests and medical supplies were sold in various provinces of the country "without invoices and without paying taxes to the state."

Bucaram was removed from office in 1997 after being declared mentally unfit to rule, and had lived in exile in Panama for nearly two decades before returning to Ecuador in 2017.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany 'rebuilding pillars' of national security
entries.summary: Germany's interior minister has defended plans to give security agencies greater investigative powers to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, German inflation rose as the ECB reconsiders interest rates. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany 'rebuilding pillars' of national security

Published September 10, 2026last updated September 10, 2026

Germany's interior minister has defended plans to give security agencies greater investigative powers to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, German inflation rose as the ECB reconsiders interest rates. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Interior Minister Dobrindt says Germany needs stronger powers to counter drones and hybrid threats
  • Energy CEO Markus Krebb said rules designed for 'peacetime' are no longer enough against sabotage
  • German inflation rose to 2.9% in August, its highest level since late 2023
  • The increase was driven mainly by higher energy prices, especially fuel and heating oil

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday September 10, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security

Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended plans to give security authorities greater investigative powers, accusing critics of putting people's safety at risk amid what he described as a heightened threat to Germany.

Speaking during a parliamentary debate on his ministry's 2027 budget, Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union, said the proposed powers were necessary to "protect our freedom."

"The threat level is high and is coming from different places," Dobrindt said.

He pointed to an explosives-laden drone discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport as evidence of the security challenges facing Germany, adding that Russia was clearly behind the incident and that it was "not an isolated event."

Dobrindt has pushed for stronger measures against drones and hybrid threats. He said under his leadership, the federal and state governments have established a new joint drone defense center, while a Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats (GAZ Hybrid) opened in June.

"We are rebuilding the pillars of security architecture," Dobrindt said on Thursday.

The Interior Ministry's budget is set to increase by more than €950 million ($1.1 billion) to €16.7 billion ($19.5 billion).

The Federal Criminal Police Office and Federal Police are among the agencies set to receive additional personnel.

Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, which is responsible for cybersecurity, is also due to receive more funding.

Sonja Eichwede, deputy parliamentary leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, highlighted additional spending planned for the Federal Agency for Technical Relief, saying it was important for civil protection and disaster response.

Skip next section Germany sees sharp fall in asylum applications, says interior minister

Germany sees sharp fall in asylum applications, says interior minister

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended the government's tougher migration policy, pointing to a sharp fall in asylum applications and continued controls at the country's borders.

"We have turned the migration wave into a migration turnaround," Dobrindt, of the Bavarian conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), told parliament during a budget debate on Thursday.

He said first-time asylum applications were down by around 75% compared with 2024.

"That is the result of control, direction and a clear stance," Dobrindt said.

Dobrindt said Germany was no longer Europe's number one destination for irregular migration.

According to European Union asylum data released on Thursday, Germany recorded approximately 55,000 applications in the first half of 2026, making it the country with the fourth-highest number of applications.

According to Dobrindt, 60,000 attempted irregular entries had been prevented at Germany's borders since the current parliamentary term began, while 1,700 suspected people smugglers had been arrested.

He said border controls would remain in place beyond September 15.

Dobrindt said the government was pursuing the same approach at European level.

He pointed to reforms of the EU's Common European Asylum System and said Germany wanted to step up returns of people whose asylum applications had been rejected.

According to Dobrindt, 42,000 people without grounds to remain had been returned from Germany to their countries of origin.

He said the next goal was to reach agreements with third countries on so-called return hubs — centers outside the EU where rejected asylum seekers could be sent.

Skip next section What prompted the warning on infrastructure?

What prompted the warning on infrastructure?

Police this week arrested a 48-year-old man suspected of trying to sabotage power lines near coal-fired power stations in North Rhine-Westphalia, Brandenburg and Saxony.

Investigators believe he used homemade rockets to fire conductive material across high-voltage lines, causing short circuits in some cases. Several units at a power station near Bergheim, west of Cologne, were reportedly taken out of operation for several days, while two short circuits were caused at a substation near the Jänschwalde power station in Brandenburg.

Authorities have linked letters claiming responsibility for the attacks to the suspect. The letters reportedly justified the sabotage as part of a campaign against electricity generation from fossil fuels.

The case has intensified concerns about the vulnerability of Germany's critical infrastructure. This includes sectors such as energy, information technology and transport whose disruption could lead to supply shortages, public-safety problems or other serious consequences.

Skip next section German inflation rises to 2.9% on energy costs

German inflation rises to 2.9% on energy costs

Inflation in Germany rose to 2.9% in August, driven largely by sharply higher energy prices, the Federal Statistical Office confirmed on Thursday.

The annual rate was the highest since late 2023, up from 2.8% in July and 2.3% in June.

Energy prices rose 10.5% compared with August last year, accelerating from an 8.3% increase in July.

Motor fuels cost 27.7% more than a year earlier, while heating oil prices jumped 49.6%.

"Particularly noticeable was the rise in energy prices, especially for fuels, which was mainly caused by the Iran war," said Federal Statistical Office President Ruth Brand.

Other household energy costs fell, however. Electricity prices were down 5.5%, natural gas including operating costs fell 2.9% and district heating was 1.0% cheaper.

Food prices were only 0.1% higher overall than a year earlier, after a 0.4% rise in July.

Some products became significantly more expensive, including eggs, up 15.2%, fresh vegetables, up 5.2%, and fish and seafood, up 4.4%.

Butter was 29.9% cheaper, while fresh fruit fell 5.6% and dairy products 5.5%.

Inflation across the eurozone also remains above the European Central Bank's 2% target.

The ECB could raise its key interest rate on Thursday for the second time this year, from 2.25% to 2.50%. It increased rates in June for the first time in almost three years before leaving them unchanged in July.

Skip next section Power boss calls for tougher protection of infrastructure

Power boss calls for tougher protection of infrastructure

The chief executive of energy giant RWE, Markus Krebber, has called for stronger protection of Germany's critical infrastructure after a string ofsabotage attacks on the power grid in several states.

"We have to learn lessons from these experiences, and quickly," Krebber said at the energy company's summer reception in Berlin.

He said current rules and bureaucratic procedures designed for "peacetime" were no longer adequate to deal with hybrid attacks on infrastructure essential to society.

Krebber criticized transparency rules that make details of critical infrastructure publicly accessible.

"The principle should actually be secrecy instead of transparency," he said.

Companies such as RWE are allowed to monitor their own sites using technology including video sensors, Krebber said. But potential attackers often prepare outside company premises.

"We need to be able to detect threats earlier," he said, arguing that critical infrastructure should also be monitored in public areas using all available technical means.

Krebber also raised the sensitive question of what he called "physical self-defense."

If a drone were approaching and it was clear that it could cause major damage, "the solution cannot be to call 110," he said, referring to Germany's police emergency number.

He called for a broader debate on how security authorities, the public sector and companies could work more closely to protect critical infrastructure.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as the head of German energy giant RWE calls for tougher protection of critical infrastructure after suspected sabotage attacks on the power grid.

RWE Chief executive Markus Krebber said Germany needs to learn lessons quickly.

Meanwhile, inflation in Germany has risen again, pushed higher mainly by energy costs.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
entries.summary: On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate

September 10, 2026

On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.

The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

"For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.

Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years."

A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.

Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.

Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.

A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.

Strong economic ties, close relations with Russia

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.

Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.

Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.

Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections."

Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.

"What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines.

Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: August hottest month ever recorded, says EU monitor
entries.summary: The average global temperature in August broke the previous record set in 2023. Climate scientists say record summer heat in the northern hemisphere and warmer oceans are all part of a new normal.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

August hottest month ever recorded, says EU monitor

September 10, 2026

The average global temperature in August broke the previous record set in 2023. Climate scientists say record summer heat in the northern hemisphere and warmer oceans are all part of a new normal.

Data from the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service released Thursday showed the average global air temperature last month measured 16.96° Celsius (62.53° F), the highest monthly global average ever recorded.

"Humans haven't seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years," Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.

Copernicus data, which goes back to 1940, recorded the previous all-time monthly high only three years ago in July 2023.

Western Europe records hottest summer

Western Europe recorded its hottest summer on record this year after successive heatwaves, droughts and wildfires.

Between mid-July and mid-August, Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat, according to estimates from the EuroMomo monitoring platform.

Additionally, ocean temperatures also tied their record high, which extended a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world's oceans.

These warm ocean temperatures come at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.

Added to this, what is estimated to be the strongest El Nino in the modern era is set to bring unusually warm Pacific waters, raising the odds of extreme weather across the world, from floods to droughts and wildfires.

Scientists point to climate change

Scientists primarily attributed the extreme heat primarily to human-caused climate change. 

"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiraling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said in response to the Copernicus report.

Stiell said "until humanity stops burning" coal, oil and gas, extreme heat would continue to break records.

Long-term warming currently averages at about 1.4°C higher than pre-industrial levels, just under the 1.5°C limit envisioned under the Paris Agreement. 

Last week, the UN said the 1.5°C goal was no longer achievable and urged faster greenhouse gas cuts.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler told the Associated Press.

"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

entries.title: Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
entries.summary: The US president gave a wide-ranging speech at the Republican midterm convention. He defended the war in Iran, trade wars and tariffs, and the White House ballroom. He also called Democrats evil and immigrants animals.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

September 10, 2026

The US president gave a wide-ranging speech at the Republican midterm convention. He defended the war in Iran, trade wars and tariffs, and the White House ballroom. He also called Democrats evil and immigrants animals.

US President Donald Trump made a pitch to voters on Wednesday: a $5,000 (€4,300) "dividend" for every American adult if the Republican Party keeps control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.

"If the Republicans win ​the House of Representatives ​and ‌the United States Senate, both of them ... because of ‌our tremendous strength and success ‌economically, ​I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the ​United States of America for $5,000," Trump said at the ⁠Republican midterm ​convention on Wednesday.

"The only caveat we have is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America," he added. "We don't want you going to Canada spending the money, we don't want you going to China or Germany."

The president did not say how he would finance the measure, nor how the government would track where citizens spend the funds. He had previously promised citizens $2,000 checks from tariff revenues that have so far not materialized.

What else did Trump talk about?

Trump made the announcement as the two-day event kicked off in Dallas, Texas.

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump talked up some of the biggest — and most divisive — aspects of his second term in office, including the crackdown on immigration, the war in Iran, tariffs and subsequent economic retaliation, the White House ballroom, and restrictions on transgender people.

The president told voters to "pretend” that he's on the ballot at the elections that will see new representatives and senators elected in November.

His attempts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario after America were met with rapturous applause. Later, he riffed on renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait."

Who else was at the Republican convention?

Other speakers focused less on the Trump administration's track record and instead attacked Democrats as "evil," "communists" and "socialists."

Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race against rising Democratic challenger James Talarico, who represents a younger and more progressive wing of that party.

Another Republican senator, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, was introduced by his Democratic counterpart, John Fetterman, in an unusual move.

Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with Democratic Party positions in recent years, introduced the Republican as his "great friend" and pledged to work with Trump to protect the state's steel industry.

Conservative activists were also in attendance.

The Associated Press spotted Stewart Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers extremist group. Rhodes had been sentenced to 18 years in prison for his role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the US Capitol, but later benefited from Trump's sweeping clemency after he returned to office.

Trump also praised Erika Kirk for being in attendance on the eve of the one-year anniversary of the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk.

Vice President JD Vance received a brief shoutout near the end of the speech.

entries.title: Philippines: Several killed, dozens missing after fire on ferry
entries.summary: Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames as rescuers brought bodies ashore in body bags. The ship's manifest listed 134 passengers and crew.
entries.content:
Philippines

Philippines: Several killed, dozens missing after ferry fire

September 10, 2026

Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames as rescuers brought bodies ashore in body bags. The ship's manifest listed 134 passengers and crew.

At least five people were killed and 87 are missing after a ferry caught fire in the Philippine province of Palawan, the Coast Guard said on Thursday.

The incident aboard the MV June Aster occurred on Wednesday evening about 2.2 kilometers (1.3 miles) off the shore of the municipality of Coron, where it was headed after departing from Baseco ​in Manila.

Coast Guard officials said 42 people had been rescued, including 38 passengers and four crew members.

Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames, and bodies placed in body bags.

The ship's manifest listed 134 people onboard, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.

"Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 87 people who are unaccounted for," Coast Guard Captain Noemi Cayabyab said on Thursday, adding that the figures could change as search and rescue operations continued.

entries.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
entries.summary: A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone

September 9, 2026

A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone.

"His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa.

Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway.

Moldova's government spokesperson said later on Wednesday that the flight was delayed when the country's airspace was closed over a drone alert. The spokesperson said in a statement that Zelenskyy's plane was able to depart after a Russian drone came down on Moldovan territory.

The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald.

Russian drone in Moldova

Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident.

A claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source.

According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday.

The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed.

However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store and the Moldovan government spokesperson.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
